lead: Landing gear and flaps move only when the aircraft is in the right state, and the stall system watches angle of attack to warn or act before lift is lost. Gear control selects up or down travel, locks the leg in place and shows the crew the result. Flap control moves trailing-edge Fowler flaps in steps and stops a split or skew. The stall computer compares angle of attack, flap position and air data with a limit, then shakes the stick as a warning and pushes it as protection. These functions are used on every take-off, approach and landing.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for gear structure and brakes, Chapter 2.1 for hydraulic actuation, Unit 1 for flight controls and Unit 3 for air data.

blocks.text: The gear selector is a lever or switch in the cockpit. It sends an electrical command to the gear control unit. The unit opens the hydraulic path to the actuators; the hydraulics are in Chapter 2.1. Up selection retracts the leg. An uplock is a hook that holds the leg in the bay after pressure is removed. Down selection extends the leg. A downlock is a spring-loaded hook that holds the leg straight for landing. Lock switches tell the control unit that the hook has engaged.

A squat switch on the shock strut closes under aircraft weight. On the ground it prevents retraction and arms the warning. In flight it reports the air state. Position switches drive green lamps for down and locked and red lamps for in transit or unlocked. A press-to-test button checks the lamps.

The gear warning sounds when the gear is not down and locked and engine power is low. Power comes from the throttle setting. A low-power approach with the gear up gives a horn or voice message. High power with the gear up may inhibit the warning, so the crew must still check gear state. The warning depends on both gear position and power.
If hydraulic pressure is lost, alternate extension releases the uplocks and lets the gear fall. Springs, compressed gas or a hand crank may be used. Gravity and air load complete the downlock.

sections.h3: Flap selection, asymmetry and load limiting

blocks.text: Trailing-edge Fowler flaps increase wing camber and wing area. The flap selector has detents such as UP, 1, 2, 3 and FULL. Each detent sets a target position. A flap control unit commands the drive motor. Limit switches at each target stop the drive when the flap reaches the selected position.

Both wings must move together. A skew sensor detects one flap surface moving out of step with the other flap surface on the same wing, for example after a drive failure. An asymmetry detector compares left and right flap angles. If the difference exceeds a small threshold, the control unit stops both drives. A split flap would roll the aircraft, so stopping is safer than completing the selection.

Load limiting protects the structure. At high airspeed the air load on the flaps is large. The control unit may limit flap travel or prevent the next step until airspeed falls. Limit switches also stop the drive at full up and full down.

Angle of attack α is the angle between the wing chord line and the relative airflow. Lift rises with α until the wing stalls at the critical angle. A stall depends on α, not on speed alone. A light aircraft can stall at high speed in a steep turn.

The angle of attack vane is a small weathercock vane on the fuselage side. It turns with the local airflow, and a rotary position transducer sends α to the stall warning computer. The computer also receives flap position and calibrated airspeed from the air data computer. It compares α with a limit that changes with flap setting.

At a set margin above the stall angle, the computer drives the stick shaker. An electric motor turns an unbalanced weight on the control column, and the column vibrates. A warning horn or voice call may sound at the same time. The shaker is a warning: it tells the crew to lower the nose.

If the crew does not respond, the stick pusher moves the column forward. An actuator pushes the control column or linkage. The pusher is protection: it reduces α even if the crew delays. It must be inhibited near the ground so it cannot push during take-off or landing. The alpha floor function in the autothrottle commands maximum thrust when α reaches a high limit; it is protection by thrust, not by pitch.

examples.question: An aircraft has a stall speed of 120 kt at mass 50 000 kg. For a fixed configuration, stall speed varies as √mass. Find the stall speed at 40 000 kg. Set the low-speed stall warning at 1.15 times the stall speed and find the warning speed.
steps: New stall speed = 120 × 0.894427 = 107.331 kt, so 107.3 kt.
examples.answer: The stall speed at 40 000 kg is 107.3 kt, and the warning speed at 1.15 times stall is 123.4 kt.
examples.check:
import math
m1 = 50000.0
m2 = 40000.0
V1 = 120.0
ratio = m2 / m1
V2 = V1 * math.sqrt(ratio)
Vw = V2 * 1.15
print(round(V2, 1))
print(round(Vw, 1))

traps: Do not swap the stick shaker and stick pusher. The shaker warns; the pusher acts.
The gear warning needs low power as well as gear up. Gear up alone does not always sound it.
A squat switch is not a gear position lock switch. It senses weight on the strut.
Flap asymmetry stops the drive; it does not continue to the selected detent.
Stall depends on angle of attack, not only on airspeed; a high-speed steep turn can stall.

quiz.q: What does the stick shaker do?
quiz.a: It vibrates the control column as a stall warning.

quiz.q: State two functions of gear downlock switches.
quiz.a: They confirm down and locked and light the green lamps. They also signal the control unit to cut hydraulic pressure to the actuators and to interlock retraction until the switch is released.

quiz.q: Why does flap asymmetry detection stop both flaps instead of driving the lagging flap to catch up?
quiz.a: A split flap creates roll. Stopping both drives limits the asymmetry and keeps control.

quiz.q: A wing stalls at α = 16°. The warning margin is 3°. At what α does the shaker start?
Mass 60 000 kg gives stall speed 130 kt. Using V ∝ √m, find the stall speed at 48 000 kg.
Why is the stick pusher inhibited near the ground?
quiz.a: It could force the nose down at low height during take-off or landing. The warning is enough there; protection must not create a hazard.

quiz.q: An aircraft with gear up and high power on final does not sound the gear warning. Is the system faulty? Explain.
quiz.a: Not necessarily. The warning needs gear not down and low power; high power may inhibit it. The crew must still check gear state.

quiz.q: How do limit switches stop the flap drive at the selected position?
quiz.a: The limit switch signals the control unit that the target position is reached. The control unit then opens the motor contactor and the drive stops. In simple light-aircraft systems the limit switch itself breaks the motor circuit.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern airliners use flight control computers to blend stall protection with envelope protection, as in alpha protection and alpha floor. Research looks at synthetic angle of attack from inertial and air data, and at preventing nuisance shakers from sensor faults. Search for angle of attack limiting, alpha floor, flap asymmetry detection and stick pusher inhibit logic.
